newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin was "run into ground" - former confidante.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin was "run into ground" - former confidante.

text.p: Top-level infighting in Russia took a new twist on Friday when Boris Yeltsin's former friend and bodyguard accused the president's current entourage of intentionally "running him into the ground".

"Some people who are now in the president's entourage really wanted to run him into the ground in order to get the situation which we have now," Lieutenant-General Alexander Korzhakov told his first news conference.
"And, naturally, they wanted to manipulate behind his back after that," he said, making clear he was referring to Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais.

Korzhakov, 46, seen as a political hawk, was dramatically sacked by his friend Yeltsin on June 18, two days after the first inconclusive round of presidential elections. Before that, he had publicly advocated postponing the poll.
"What we have now is that power, in an apparently legitimate way, has gone into the hands of those never elected in a legitimate way," Korzhakov said.
"We have got an unconstitutional institution of regency while the president is alive. The president has fewer and fewer levers of power left in his hands."
There was no immediate comment from Chubais.
Yeltsin disappeared from view soon after the first round of the presidential election. On September 5 he said he had decided to have heart surgery and hoped to return to active life.
Doctors have since been preparing him for the operation, first in hospital and now at a country sanatorium near Moscow.

Chubais played a pivotal role in an energetic, U.S.-style meet-the-people campaign which won Yeltsin another four years in the Kremlin. Korzhakov was sacked after Chubais accused him of trying to derail the election.
Korzhakov said the campaign had destroyed Yeltsin's health.
"I had a very long chat with Boris Nikolayevich (during the campaign) in which he expressed great concern that he would not be able to stand this race," Korzhakov said.
"He was very tired by then because of constant travel, meetings with people, speeches, dances. A real threat to his health emerged."
Korzhakov, a bull-like figure of a man, stood by Yeltsin through good times and bad for 11 years.
Yeltsin's tennis, swimming and -- some say -- drinking partner, the former KGB officer was seen by the Russian media as an extremely influential figure in the intrigue-filled world of the Kremlin.
He is now desperately trying to launch a political career of his own and intends to stand in a parliamentary by-election in the central region of Tula.
The position became vacant after Yeltsin named general Alexander Lebed, who held it, his national security chief.

Korzhakov's news conference turned into a media circus as journalists ignored a parliamentary debate on the 1997 budget and jammed into a room much too small for them to watch the latest development in a smear campaign rocking Russian politics.
Many commentators see the row as a ghastly turn in a struggle between top figures manouevring for power while Yeltsin prepares for surgery.
The mudslinging involves Korzhakov, some of his former trustees, powerful bankers, the mass media they control, Lebed and his professed foe, Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov.
Much of the Russian media say "compromising material" is being used to prevent a possible alliance between Lebed, who does not hide his presidential ambitions, and Korzhakov.
Korzhakov said on Friday Lebed had "the best political future in the country" but played down his own importance.

He also dismissed accusations, made by a former top businessman, of a multi-million-dollar extortion demand. The businessman, Boris Fyodorov, appeared at the news conference but was ousted by security.
